title: National Right to Work Committee Formed: Corporate Anti-Union Infrastructure Nationalized
description: Following passage of the Taft-Hartley Act in 1947, former Congressman Fred Hartley (co-author of Taft-Hartley) and a group of business leaders form the National Right to Work Committee (NRTWC) along with the National Right to Work Legal Defense Fund. The organizations' stated goals are to pass right-to-work laws in all 50 states and eliminate organized labor. Section 14(b) of the Taft-Hartley Act explicitly grants states the right to enact right-to-work laws, providing federal authorization for the state-level corporate campaigns. The NRTWC nationalizes and coordinates what had been regional corporate anti-union efforts led by organizations like Vance Muse's Christian American Association and state-level business groups. By bringing Hartley—co-author of the foundational anti-labor legislation—into leadership, the NRTWC demonstrates direct continuity between federal anti-labor policy and state-level corporate organizing. The creation of both a lobbying organization (NRTWC) and a legal defense fund shows sophisticated multi-pronged strategy: legislative campaigns and litigation support. This infrastructure enables corporate interests to systematically weaken unions state-by-state over subsequent decades.
actors: National Right to Work Legal Defense Fund

sources.title: The History of Right to Work, 75 Years Later

significance: Creates permanent national infrastructure for corporate anti-union campaigns, coordinating state-level efforts that had previously been regional. The dual structure (lobbying committee + legal defense fund) becomes model for later corporate political organizations. Fred Hartley's leadership provides direct link between federal anti-labor legislation (Taft-Hartley) and state implementation, showing coordinated multi-level strategy. The organization's explicitly stated goal to 'eliminate organized labor' demonstrates corporate willingness to openly pursue destruction of union power. NRTWC's ongoing influence (active through 2025) shows success in creating durable anti-labor infrastructure.
